claim: Muscle spindles are encapsulated sensory organs found in most of our muscles.
source: Muscle spindles are encapsulated sensory organs found in most of our muscles.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Prevalent models of sensorimotor control assume the role of spindles is to reliably encode limb posture and movement.
source: Prevalent models of sensorimotor control assume the role of spindles is to reliably encode limb posture and movement.
evidence: This claim references existing models in the field, representing established views in the literature.

claim: Spindle organs can be tuned by spinal γ motor neurons that receive top-down and peripheral input, including from cutaneous afferents.
source: Spindle organs can be tuned by spinal γ motor neurons that receive top-down and peripheral input, including from cutaneous afferents.
evidence: This is presented as an established fact about spindle physiology, drawing on known anatomical and physiological knowledge.

claim: Spindles play a unique overarching role in the nervous system as peripheral signal-processing devices that flexibly facilitate sensorimotor performance according to task characteristics.
source: I propose that spindles play a unique overarching role in the nervous system: that of a peripheral signal-processing device that flexibly facilitates sensorimotor performance, according to task characteristics.
evidence: This is the author's main theoretical proposal, supported by inference from the studies described.

claim: Spindle tuning enables the independent preparatory control of reflex muscle stiffness.
source: Such studies have so far shown that spindle tuning enables the independent preparatory control of reflex muscle stiffness, the selective extraction of information during implicit motor adaptation, and for segmental stretch reflexes to operate in joint space.
evidence: This claim is supported by recent studies with naturalistically active humans, as stated in the abstract.

claim: Spindle tuning enables the selective extraction of information during implicit motor adaptation.
source: Such studies have so far shown that spindle tuning enables the independent preparatory control of reflex muscle stiffness, the selective extraction of information during implicit motor adaptation, and for segmental stretch reflexes to operate in joint space.
evidence: This claim is supported by recent studies with naturalistically active humans, as stated in the abstract.

claim: Spindle tuning enables segmental stretch reflexes to operate in joint space.
source: Such studies have so far shown that spindle tuning enables the independent preparatory control of reflex muscle stiffness, the selective extraction of information during implicit motor adaptation, and for segmental stretch reflexes to operate in joint space.
evidence: This claim is supported by recent studies with naturalistically active humans, as stated in the abstract.

claim: Spindles are generally believed to be basic mechanoreceptors that encode muscle stretch and provide reliable information about actual limb posture and movement kinematics.
source: Spindles are generally believed to be basic mechanoreceptors that encode muscle stretch and provide reliable information about actual limb posture and movement kinematics.
evidence: This represents the traditional view in the field, based on established scientific consensus.

claim: Previous work has added knowledge about the molecular mechanisms of mechanotransduction in spindles.
source: Previous work and more recent studies using genetic manipulation methods have added a great deal of knowledge about the molecular mechanisms of mechanotransduction (e.g. Kruse and Poppele, 1991; Bewick and Banks, 2015; Woo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Spindles have been proposed to play a basic, low-level role in reflex motor control.
source: Spindles have been proposed to play a basic, low-level role in reflex motor control (Houk, 1976) and proprioception (Goodwin et al., 1972), and their malfunction has been linked to impaired motor coordination (Sainburg et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Houk, 1976.

claim: Spindles have been proposed to play a role in proprioception.
source: Spindles have been proposed to play a basic, low-level role in reflex motor control (Houk, 1976) and proprioception (Goodwin et al., 1972), and their malfunction has been linked to impaired motor coordination (Sainburg et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Goodwin et al., 1972.

claim: Spindle malfunction has been linked to impaired motor coordination.
source: Spindles have been proposed to play a basic, low-level role in reflex motor control (Houk, 1976) and proprioception (Goodwin et al., 1972), and their malfunction has been linked to impaired motor coordination (Sainburg et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sainburg et al., 1993.

claim: The mechanoreceptive part of spindles responds best to force-related variables in relaxed muscles.
source: An interesting recent proposition is that the mechanoreceptive part of spindles responds best to force-related variables, as shown in relaxed muscles (Blum et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blum et al., 2017.

claim: The role of muscle spindle organs in their entirety under in vivo efferent control has remained unclear.
source: Still, the role of muscle spindle organs in their entirety (i.e. of the mechanoreceptor under in vivo efferent control) has remained unclear(for a recent comprehensive review see Macefield and Knellwolf, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge, with reference to a comprehensive review.

claim: There are two main types of muscle spindle receptors: primary and secondary.
source: Specifically, there are two main types of muscle spindle receptors, the primary and the secondary, which give rise to the primary (type Ia) and secondary (type II) afferents, respectively (Boyd and Davidson, 1997).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Primary spindle receptors give rise to type Ia afferents.
source: Specifically, there are two main types of muscle spindle receptors, the primary and the secondary, which give rise to the primary (type Ia) and secondary (type II) afferents, respectively (Boyd and Davidson, 1997).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Secondary spindle receptors give rise to type II afferents.
source: Specifically, there are two main types of muscle spindle receptors, the primary and the secondary, which give rise to the primary (type Ia) and secondary (type II) afferents, respectively (Boyd and Davidson, 1997).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: During ramp-and-hold stretch of relaxed muscle, type Ia afferents are most responsive during muscle stretch and are sensitive to the rate of change of length.
source: When imposing a ramp-and-hold stretch of the relaxed muscle, type Ia from this muscle are most responsive during muscle stretch, are sensitive to the rate of change of length (i.e., velocity), may encode static length but are silent during muscle shortening.
evidence: This describes established physiological responses of type Ia afferents.

claim: Type Ia afferents may encode static length but are silent during muscle shortening.
source: When imposing a ramp-and-hold stretch of the relaxed muscle, type Ia from this muscle are most responsive during muscle stretch, are sensitive to the rate of change of length (i.e., velocity), may encode static length but are silent during muscle shortening.
evidence: This describes established physiological responses of type Ia afferents.

claim: Under passive conditions, primary spindle afferents have both good dynamic and fairly good static muscle-length sensitivity.
source: That is, under passive conditions, primaries can be considered to have both a good dynamic and fairly good static muscle-length sensitivity, whereas type II from passive muscle represent good static length sensitivity but a poorer dynamic sensitivity (Edin and Vallbo, 1990a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Edin and Vallbo, 1990a.

claim: Type II afferents from passive muscle represent good static length sensitivity but poorer dynamic sensitivity.
source: That is, under passive conditions, primaries can be considered to have both a good dynamic and fairly good static muscle-length sensitivity, whereas type II from passive muscle represent good static length sensitivity but a poorer dynamic sensitivity (Edin and Vallbo, 1990a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Edin and Vallbo, 1990a.

claim: Spindle organs have their own motor supply in the form of γ motor (fusimotor) neurons.
source: However, unlike other types of peripheral mechanoreceptors, the spindle organs have their own motor supply in the form of γ motor ('fusimotor') neurons (Barker and Chin, 1961; Matthews, 1972).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The overarching role of muscle spindles in sensorimotor control has remained unclear, particularly in the context of naturalistic active movement.
source: Despite their rich innervation, the overarching role of muscle spindles in sensorimotor control has remained unclear, particularly so in the context of naturalistic active movement.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current understanding.

claim: Prevalent models of sensorimotor control view mechanoreceptors in muscle and skin as basic sensors that transduce physical stimuli into unimodal feedback signals.
source: This framework views mechanoreceptors in muscle and skin as basic sensors that transduce physical stimuli into unimodal feedback signals, ignoring the independent motor supply to muscle spindles.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Prevalent models of sensorimotor control ignore the independent motor supply to muscle spindles.
source: This framework views mechanoreceptors in muscle and skin as basic sensors that transduce physical stimuli into unimodal feedback signals, ignoring the independent motor supply to muscle spindles.
evidence: This is a critique of existing models based on what they omit.

claim: In mammals, approximately 30% of spinal motor neurons are γ motor neurons.
source: However, in mammals, ~30% of spinal motor neurons are γ, which supply muscle spindles exclusively (Kuffler et al., 1951; Burke et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuffler et al., 1951 and Burke et al., 1977.

claim: γ motor neurons supply muscle spindles exclusively.
source: However, in mammals, ~30% of spinal motor neurons are γ, which supply muscle spindles exclusively (Kuffler et al., 1951; Burke et al., 1977).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: γ motor neurons can be controlled by descending commands and/or peripheral afferent input.
source: These γ neurons can be controlled by descending commands and/or peripheral afferent input (Figure 1B; see also following sections).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The nervous system has placed a premium on the control of muscle spindle signals at source.
source: The nervous system has clearly placed a premium on the control of muscle spindle signals at source.
evidence: This is inferred from the large proportion of motor neurons dedicated to spindle control.

claim: α-γ co-activation is the most popularized explanation for human spindle control.
source: The most popularized explanation for human spindle control is based on 'α-γ co-activation' (Vallbo, 1970).
evidence: This is stated as a well-known concept in the field, supported by citation.

claim: In the α-γ co-activation view, γ fusimotor neurons are activated virtually the same time as α motor neurons to prevent spindles from falling slack during muscle contraction.
source: In this view, γ fusimotor neurons are activated virtually the same time as α motor neurons, in order to prevent spindles from falling slack during muscle contraction.
evidence: This describes the traditional α-γ co-activation model.

claim: Most support for lack of independence between α and γ motor neuron activity has come from recording spindle afferent signals during isometric contractions or during unnaturally slow and restricted movements.
source: Most support for a lack of independence between α and γ motor neuron activity has come from recording spindle afferent signals during isometric contractions or during unnaturally slow and restricted movements (e.g. Gandevia and Burke, 1985; Wessberg and Vallbo, 1995; Kakuda et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Co-activation of extrafusal and intrafusal muscle fibers can be easily implemented through beta neurons.
source: Moreover, co-activation of extrafusal (skeletal) and intrafusal (spindle) muscle fibers can be easily implemented through the more primitive beta neurons (Jami et al., 1982; Emonet-Dénand et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jami et al., 1982 and Emonet-Dénand et al., 1992.

claim: β motor neurons are essentially α motor neurons that branch out to innervate extrafusal and intrafusal muscle fibers.
source: β neurons are essentially just α motor neurons that branch out to innervate extrafusal and intrafusal muscle fibers.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Both mammals and lower vertebrates have β motor neurons.
source: Both mammals and lower vertebrates have β motor neurons, but only mammals seem to have γ motor neurons (Hunt, 1951; Emonet-Dénand and Laporte, 1975; Murthy, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative anatomy studies.

claim: Only mammals seem to have γ motor neurons.
source: Both mammals and lower vertebrates have β motor neurons, but only mammals seem to have γ motor neurons (Hunt, 1951; Emonet-Dénand and Laporte, 1975; Murthy, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative anatomy studies.

claim: The vast majority of efferent projections to mammalian spindles are from γ motor neurons.
source: The vast majority of efferent projections to mammalian spindles are from γ motor neurons (Matthews, 1964; Emonet-Dénand et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Matthews, 1964 and Emonet-Dénand et al., 1992.

claim: The independent γ motor supply represents an evolutionary advantage realized through the ability to dissociate spindle control from the control of skeletal muscles.
source: The independent γ motor supply must therefore represent an evolutionary advantage, realized through the ability to dissociate spindle control from the control of skeletal muscles, in cases where this dissociation is favorable to the organism (see following sections).
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary reasoning and comparative anatomy.

claim: α-γ co-activation can account for the increase in spindle afferent firing observed during isometric contraction of the spindle-bearing muscle.
source: Nevertheless, α-γ co-activation can account for the increase in spindle afferent firing observed during isometric contraction of the spindle-bearing muscle (Edin and Vallbo, 1990b); β motor neurons can also contribute (Kakuda et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Edin and Vallbo, 1990b and Kakuda et al., 1998.

claim: The increase in spindle firing during isometric contraction is congruent with automatic gain-scaling of short-latency stretch reflexes.
source: This increase in spindle firing is congruent with the known 'automatic' gain-scaling of short-latency stretch reflexes (SLRs), where reflex sensitivity is proportional to background activation of the homonymous muscle, as shown in postural tasks (e.g. Matthews, 1986; Pruszynski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Matthews, 1986 and Pruszynski et al., 2009.

claim: Automatic gain-scaling alone cannot account for the modulation of SLR gains observed during movement.
source: However, automatic gain-scaling alone cannot account for the modulation of SLR gains observed during movement (Dufresne et al., 1980; Soechting et al., 1981; Nakazawa et al., 1997; Wallace and Miles, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing SLR modulation during movement.

claim: Spindle sensitivity to stretch can be positively related to the activity level of the spindle-bearing muscle and negatively related to antagonist muscle activity.
source: I have recently shown that spindle sensitivity to stretch can be positively related to the activity level of the spindle-bearing muscle, but also be negatively related to antagonist muscle activity (Dimitriou, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the author's own published data.

claim: During continuous sinusoidal movements of a finger against different loads, spindle responsiveness to stretch depends on the balance of activity across an antagonistic muscle pair rather than activity in the spindle-bearing muscle alone.
source: That is, during continuous sinusoidal movements of a finger against different loads, spindle responsiveness to stretch was shown to depend on the balance of activity across an antagonistic muscle pair (hence joint dynamics), rather than activity in the spindle-bearing muscle alone (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A from Dimitriou, 2014.

claim: The negative relationship between spindle sensitivity and antagonist activation is compatible with top-down reciprocal inhibition of fusimotor neurons.
source: The negative relationship with antagonist activation is compatible with top-down reciprocal inhibition of fusimotor neurons, as shown in intercostal muscles of the cat (Sears, 1964).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Sears, 1964.

claim: Villamar et al., 2021 tested the hypothesis that SLR sensitivity during movement can be explained by the balance of activity across agonist and antagonist muscles.
source: Using an innovative experimental approach, Villamar et al., 2021 have very recently tested the hypothesis that SLR sensitivity during movement can be explained by the balance of activity across agonist and antagonist muscles.
evidence: This is a direct reference to a specific study.

claim: The observed changes in SLR sensitivity during ballistic elbow movements reflected the net background activity across agonist and antagonist muscles.
source: The observed changes in SLR sensitivity during ballistic elbow movements did reflect the net background activity across agonist and antagonist muscles.
evidence: This is a finding from Villamar et al., 2021.

claim: The relative impact of agonist and antagonist activity on SLR gain were remarkably similar to the coefficients generated by the spindle study.
source: Moreover, the relative impact of agonist and antagonist activity on SLR gain were 'remarkably similar' to the coefficients generated by the aforementioned spindle study.
evidence: This is a finding from Villamar et al., 2021 compared to Dimitriou, 2014.

claim: Spindle tuning is at least partly responsible for shaping SLR gains during sinusoidal and ballistic movements under different loads.
source: Although the contribution of other mechanisms cannot be excluded, taken together, the afferent and stretch reflex results suggest that spindle tuning is at least partly responsible for shaping SLR gains during sinusoidal and ballistic movements under different loads.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined results from multiple studies.

claim: In the context of sinusoidal and ballistic single-joint movement, primary spindles do not function as reliable unimodal sensors encoding muscle stretch or joint rotation.
source: In the context of sinusoidal and ballistic single-joint movement, primary spindles do not seem to function as reliable unimodal sensors encoding muscle stretch or joint rotation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Spindle tuning based on muscle activation balance enables segmental reflex contribution from single muscles to occur in joint space.
source: That is, spindle tuning based on muscle activation balance (i.e. reciprocal control) enables even segmental reflex contribution from single muscles to occur in 'joint space'.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spindle tuning data.

claim: Neither α-γ co-activation nor antagonistic muscle balance can justify the need for an independent fusimotor system.
source: However, neither 'α-γ co-activation' nor 'antagonistic muscle balance' can justify the need for an independent fusimotor system.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of these mechanisms.

claim: Recording from individual spindle afferents using microneurography is a feasible and preferable alternative to recording from γ motor neurons.
source: However, recording from individual spindle afferents using microneurography is a feasible and even preferable alternative, because γ neurons supply spindles exclusively, and the spindle organ acts as an integrator of input from mechanoreception and multiple fusimotor fibers; that is, afferent firing also allows assessment of net fusimotor impact, whereas random fusimotor fibers, whose actions sum non-linearly, may be less revealing in this respect (Matthews, 1972; Prochazka, 1989).
evidence: This is a methodological argument supported by citations.

claim: The spindle organ acts as an integrator of input from mechanoreception and multiple fusimotor fibers.
source: However, recording from individual spindle afferents using microneurography is a feasible and even preferable alternative, because γ neurons supply spindles exclusively, and the spindle organ acts as an integrator of input from mechanoreception and multiple fusimotor fibers; that is, afferent firing also allows assessment of net fusimotor impact, whereas random fusimotor fibers, whose actions sum non-linearly, may be less revealing in this respect (Matthews, 1972; Prochazka, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about spindle physiology supported by citations.

claim: In the visuomotor rotation task, participants used their right hand while spindle afferent signals were recorded from wrist extensor muscles.
source: In a recent study, participants used their right hand to perform this task while spindle afferent signals were recorded from wrist extensor muscles (Dimitriou, 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup from Dimitriou, 2016.

claim: The observed adaptation behavior in the visuomotor rotation task was stereotypical, with an exponential curve fitted to movement direction error in early adaptation and washout.
source: The observed adaptation behavior was stereotypical for this type of task: an exponential curve could be fitted to movement direction error in the early adaptation stage and in 'washout' (the stage where participants gradually re-adapt to removal of the visual distortion).
evidence: This describes the behavioral results from Dimitriou, 2016.

claim: Despite fundamentally identical muscle kinematics across all stages of the visuomotor rotation task, there was a dissociation in spindle population signals as a function of task stage.
source: Despite fundamentally identical muscle kinematics across all stages of the task, there was a dissociation in spindle population signals as a function of task stage.
evidence: This is a key finding from Dimitriou, 2016.

claim: Compared to baseline, there was an increase in primary muscle spindle sensitivity to stretch in early adaptation.
source: Specifically, compared to baseline, there was an increase in primary muscle spindle sensitivity to stretch in early adaptation (Figure 2B) suggesting a similar increase in stretch reflex gains as a means of reducing movement error online.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B from Dimitriou, 2016.

claim: In the washout stage, spindle afferents stopped encoding stretch velocity and were linearized with respect to muscle length.
source: In the washout stage, spindle afferents (Ia and II) stopped encoding stretch velocity and were instead 'linearized' with respect to muscle length (Figure 2BC, green).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and 2C from Dimitriou, 2016.

claim: Spindle signals were tuned to hand position only during washout, possibly for facilitating the relevant update of internal models.
source: That is, spindle signals were tuned to hand position only during washout, possibly for facilitating the relevant update of internal models in this stage, where haptic and visual coordinate frames re-align.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from Dimitriou, 2016.

claim: A follow-up study applied whole-arm perturbations during probe trials randomly interleaved at different stages of the implicit adaptation task and produced equivalent findings concerning stretch reflex tuning.
source: A follow-up study applied whole-arm perturbations during probe trials that were randomly interleaved at the different stages of the implicit adaptation task; the study produced equivalent findings concerning stretch reflex tuning, including evidence that levels of SLR attenuation in washout (a proxy for spindle 'linearization') reflect individual rates of implicit adaptation (Dimitriou, 2018).
evidence: This describes findings from Dimitriou, 2018.

claim: Levels of SLR attenuation in washout reflect individual rates of implicit adaptation.
source: A follow-up study applied whole-arm perturbations during probe trials that were randomly interleaved at the different stages of the implicit adaptation task; the study produced equivalent findings concerning stretch reflex tuning, including evidence that levels of SLR attenuation in washout (a proxy for spindle 'linearization') reflect individual rates of implicit adaptation (Dimitriou, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from Dimitriou, 2018.

claim: Flexible and adaptive motor control can rely on statistically optimal integration of multimodal sensory inputs.
source: It is believed that flexible and adaptive motor control can rely on statistically optimal integration of multimodal sensory inputs (e.g. Körding and Wolpert, 2004; Bays and Wolpert, 2007).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: For reaching movements, proprioceptive and visual information are thought to be weighted according to their direction-dependent precision.
source: For reaching movements, proprioceptive and visual information are thought to be weighted according to their direction-dependent precision (van Beers et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Beers et al., 1999.

claim: The brain constructs flexible coordinate representations depending on task needs and characteristics.
source: Another line of research suggests that the brain constructs flexible coordinate representations depending on task needs and characteristics (Bernier and Grafton, 2010; McGuire and Sabes, 2011; Leoné et al., 2015), although the required coordinate transformations are considered costly due error and noise in the underlying computations (Soechting and Flanders, 1989; Sober and Sabes, 2005; Schlicht and Schrater, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Coordinate transformations are considered costly due to error and noise in the underlying computations.
source: Another line of research suggests that the brain constructs flexible coordinate representations depending on task needs and characteristics (Bernier and Grafton, 2010; McGuire and Sabes, 2011; Leoné et al., 2015), although the required coordinate transformations are considered costly due error and noise in the underlying computations (Soechting and Flanders, 1989; Sober and Sabes, 2005; Schlicht and Schrater, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soechting and Flanders, 1989; Sober and Sabes, 2005; Schlicht and Schrater, 2007.

claim: By siphoning multimodal information to the periphery to construct flexible representations at source, spindles and their fusimotor control may help alleviate some of the cost associated with internal coordinate transformations.
source: By siphoning multimodal information to the periphery in order to construct flexible representations at source, spindles and their fusimotor control may help alleviate some of the cost associated with internal coordinate transformations.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on inference from the data.

claim: Having a long-enough preparatory delay improves the overall quality of movement and cuts down on reaction time.
source: This delay is designed to investigate movement preparation. Having a long-enough preparatory delay improves the overall quality of movement and cuts down on reaction time (Rosenbaum, 1980; Ghez et al., 1997; Sutter et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rosenbaum, 1980; Ghez et al., 1997; Sutter et al., 2021.

claim: Preparatory cortical activity correlates well with parameters such as movement direction/extent and visual target location.
source: Preparatory cortical activity correlates well with parameters such as movement direction/extent and visual target location (Tanji and Evarts, 1976; Weinrich et al., 1984; Kurata, 1993; Shen and Alexander, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: It was initially suggested that preparatory cortical activity represents a subthreshold version of the activity seen during movement.
source: It was initially suggested that preparatory cortical activity represents a subthreshold version of the activity seen during movement, but more recent work suggests that preparation sets an initial neural state that somehow facilitates the subsequent movement (Churchland et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes an earlier hypothesis in the field.

claim: More recent work suggests that preparation sets an initial neural state that facilitates the subsequent movement.
source: It was initially suggested that preparatory cortical activity represents a subthreshold version of the activity seen during movement, but more recent work suggests that preparation sets an initial neural state that somehow facilitates the subsequent movement (Churchland et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Churchland et al., 2010.

claim: Goal-directed tuning of muscle spindles and stretch reflex gains occurs during movement preparation.
source: In a recent study (Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021), we demonstrate goal-directed tuning of muscle spindles and stretch reflex gains during movement preparation.
evidence: This is a finding from Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021.

claim: Despite no differences in kinematics or surface EMG during preparation, type Ia firing rates were lower when preparing to reach targets associated with stretch of the spindle-bearing muscle.
source: Specifically, despite no differences in kinematics or surface EMG during preparation, type Ia firing rates were lower when preparing to reach targets associated with stretch of the spindle-bearing muscle (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D from Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021.

claim: Spindle responses can be flexibly adjusted according to extrinsic visual information about target location.
source: That is, spindle responses can also be flexibly adjusted according to 'extrinsic' visual information about target location.
evidence: This is an inference from the data in Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021.

claim: The findings of goal-directed spindle tuning are congruent with recent reports of preparatory modulation in the primary somatosensory cortex.
source: These findings are congruent with recent reports of preparatory modulation in the primary somatosensory cortex (Ariani et al., 2022; Gale et al., 2021), but suggest that such preparatory changes in the CNS may be partially due to processing altered afferent signals, rather than exclusively reflect internally-generated commands or priming.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the findings to other studies, supported by citations.

claim: Preparatory changes in the CNS may be partially due to processing altered afferent signals rather than exclusively reflecting internally-generated commands.
source: These findings are congruent with recent reports of preparatory modulation in the primary somatosensory cortex (Ariani et al., 2022; Gale et al., 2021), but suggest that such preparatory changes in the CNS may be partially due to processing altered afferent signals, rather than exclusively reflect internally-generated commands or priming.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: There is a strong positive relationship between type Ia firing during late preparation and time-to-peak velocity during reaching.
source: We also found a strong positive relationship between type Ia firing during late preparation and time-to-peak velocity during reaching, suggesting that spindle preparatory tuning has a substantial impact on the subsequent voluntary movement (Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021); every additional unit increase in Ia firing rate involved a 3ms delay in attaining peak velocity during movement.
evidence: This is a finding from Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021.

claim: Every additional unit increase in Ia firing rate during late preparation involved a 3ms delay in attaining peak velocity during movement.
source: We also found a strong positive relationship between type Ia firing during late preparation and time-to-peak velocity during reaching, suggesting that spindle preparatory tuning has a substantial impact on the subsequent voluntary movement (Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021); every additional unit increase in Ia firing rate involved a 3ms delay in attaining peak velocity during movement.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021.

claim: By independently modifying spindle gains, the fusimotor system can affect the degree of reflex muscle stiffness during movement execution without affecting contractile muscle force during preparation.
source: By independently modifying spindle gains, the fusimotor system can affect the degree of reflex muscle stiffness during movement execution, without affecting contractile muscle force during preparation.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Muscle afferent (reflex) feedback contributes about a third of volitional contraction.
source: Muscle afferent (reflex) feedback contributes significantly to force generation, about a third of volitional contraction (Hagbarth et al., 1986; Gandevia et al., 1990), regardless if the contraction is maximal or not (Macefield et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hagbarth et al., 1986 and Gandevia et al., 1990.

claim: Muscle afferent feedback contributes to force generation regardless of whether the contraction is maximal or not.
source: Muscle afferent (reflex) feedback contributes significantly to force generation, about a third of volitional contraction (Hagbarth et al., 1986; Gandevia et al., 1990), regardless if the contraction is maximal or not (Macefield et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Macefield et al., 1993.

claim: Spindle Ia signals can affect long-latency stretch reflex responses.
source: It is known that spindle Ia signals can also affect long-latency stretch reflex responses - LLRs (e.g. Hunter et al., 1988; Fellows et al., 1993; Pruszynski and Scott, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Goal-directed tuning of type Ia responses reflected a congruent modulation of stretch reflex gains at all latencies, including at SLR latencies in cases where the muscle was not heavily pre-loaded.
source: Additional experiments implicating whole-arm perturbations confirmed that goal-directed tuning of type Ia responses reflected a congruent modulation of stretch reflex gains at all latencies, including at SLR latencies in cases where the muscle was not heavily pre-loaded (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E from Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021.

claim: LLR gains exhibited goal-dependency regardless of muscle pre-loading level.
source: LLR gains exhibited goal-dependency regardless of muscle pre-loading level (Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021.

claim: Goal-directed modulation of LLR gains was stronger following a long rather than a relatively short preparatory delay.
source: The same study demonstrated that goal-directed modulation of LLR gains was stronger following a long rather than a relatively short preparatory delay, closely matching the temporal evolution of spindle preparatory tuning.
evidence: This is a finding from Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021.

claim: The short preparatory delay (200-250 ms) is considerably longer than the minimum delay required for shaping LLR responses via selective CNS processing.
source: Moreover, the used 'short' preparatory delay (200–250 ms) is considerably longer than the minimum delay required for shaping LLR responses via selective CNS processing (e.g. Yang et al., 2011; Scott, 2016), but shorter than the time required for full afferent expression of changes in dynamic fusimotor drive (Crowe and Matthews, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2011; Scott, 2016; and Crowe and Matthews, 1964.

claim: The short preparatory delay is shorter than the time required for full afferent expression of changes in dynamic fusimotor drive.
source: Moreover, the used 'short' preparatory delay (200–250 ms) is considerably longer than the minimum delay required for shaping LLR responses via selective CNS processing (e.g. Yang et al., 2011; Scott, 2016), but shorter than the time required for full afferent expression of changes in dynamic fusimotor drive (Crowe and Matthews, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crowe and Matthews, 1964.

claim: In planned voluntary reach, spindle responses to stretch can be locally adjusted according to the intention to move in a particular direction.
source: Nevertheless, in planned voluntary reach, spindle responses to stretch can be locally adjusted (or 'processed') according to the intention to move in a particular direction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D from Papaioannou and Dimitriou, 2021.

claim: Tuning of human spindles can reflect specific goals within a behavioral context, which represents a finer degree of spindle modulation than tuning according to behavioral context or type of task.
source: That is, tuning of human spindles can reflect specific goals within a behavioral context (reaching), which represents a finer degree of spindle modulation than tuning according to behavioral context or type of task, as previously and more recently suggested (Prochazka et al., 1985; Ribot-Ciscar and Ackerley, 2021).
evidence: This is an inference comparing the current findings to previous work, supported by citations.

claim: One study found no evidence of a selective effect on fusimotor neurons when anticipating the need to make a contraction that would oppose an imposed movement of the foot at the ankle.
source: One study found no evidence of a selective effect on fusimotor neurons when anticipating the need to make a contraction that would oppose an imposed movement of the foot at the ankle (Burke et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burke et al., 1980.

claim: The intention to perform a voluntary goal-directed movement may be necessary for engaging independent fusimotor control.
source: In this case, the intention to perform a voluntary goal-directed movement may be necessary for engaging independent fusimotor control.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differences between studies.

claim: All findings described in Figure 2 involve control of the dominant upper limb.
source: It should be emphasized that all findings described in Figure 2 involve control of the dominant upper limb.
evidence: This is a methodological note about the scope of the findings.

claim: There may be a large degree of functional specialization in the fusimotor control of upper vs. lower limbs.
source: It is possible that there is a large degree of functional specialization in the fusimotor control of upper vs. lower limbs.
evidence: This is speculation about potential differences between limbs.

claim: Most of what we know concerning mammalian muscle spindle structure and fusimotor function has come from work with cats.
source: Most of what we know concerning mammalian muscle spindle structure and fusimotor function has come from work with cats (e.g. Barker, 1948; Matthews, 1972; Hulliger, 1984), and many inferences we currently make concerning human fusimotor control would have been impossible without this work.
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work in cats.

claim: There are two independently controlled groups of γ motor neurons: static and dynamic.
source: For example, such research has shown that there are two independently controlled groups of γ motor neurons, 'static' and 'dynamic', with the latter innervating only primary muscle spindles (Matthews, 1962).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Matthews, 1962.

claim: Dynamic γ motor neurons innervate only primary muscle spindles.
source: For example, such research has shown that there are two independently controlled groups of γ motor neurons, 'static' and 'dynamic', with the latter innervating only primary muscle spindles (Matthews, 1962).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Matthews, 1962.

claim: In active cats, fusimotor and spindle activity has been most thoroughly examined in the context of locomotion.
source: In active cats, fusimotor and spindle activity has been most thoroughly examined in the context of locomotion (see e.g. Prochazka, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prochazka, 1996.

claim: Equivalent data during human locomotion are lacking due to methodological limitations.
source: Equivalent data during human locomotion are lacking due to methodological limitations.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: Mathematical modelling suggests that fusimotor control optimizes the spindles' ability to encode position sense by accounting for musculoskeletal complexities and output noise.
source: Mathematical modelling suggests that fusimotor control optimizes the spindles' ability to encode position sense by accounting for the presence of musculoskeletal complexities and output noise (Scott and Loeb, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scott and Loeb, 1994.

claim: Spindles are independently controlled in a predictive manner to modulate the function of spinal central pattern generator circuits during locomotion.
source: However, another prominent line of work suggests that spindles are not length detectors, but instead are independently controlled in a predictive manner in order to modulate the function of spinal central pattern generator (CPG) circuits during locomotion (Ellaway et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ellaway et al., 2015.

claim: It is currently unclear whether CPG networks exist in the human spinal cord.
source: A similar fusimotor support of human bipedal locomotion may occur, although it is currently unclear whether CPG networks exist in the human spinal cord (Minassian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Minassian et al., 2017.

claim: The closest relationship between spindle firing rate and muscle velocity was observed when velocity occurred ~150ms after the spindle signal.
source: In one paper, we correlated spindle population responses recorded during block-grasping and key-pressing with muscle velocity occurring at the same time as the recorded afferent signal, and velocity observed at different points into the future (Dimitriou and Edin, 2010). The closest relationship was between afferent firing rate and velocity ~150ms after the spindle signal.
evidence: This is a finding from Dimitriou and Edin, 2010.

claim: Muscle spindles fulfilled all three neurophysiological criteria for identifying a forward sensory model.
source: This result meant that muscle spindles fulfilled all three neurophysiological criteria for identifying a forward sensory model (Wolpert and Miall, 1996): spindle inputs were the current state of the system (mechanoreception) and an efferent command (β or α-γ), and spindle output predicted the future kinematic state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Dimitriou and Edin, 2010, referencing criteria from Wolpert and Miall, 1996.

claim: The spindles' predictive capacity does not hold across tasks.
source: However, later studies showed that the spindles' 'predictive' capacity does not hold across tasks.
evidence: This is based on findings from later studies by the author.

claim: Suddenly adding a new external load did not significantly alter the predictive capacity of spindles during the initial cycles of sinusoidal movement.
source: For example, if anything, the opposite results should have been observed in preparatory modulation (e.g., Figure 2D), and suddenly adding a new external load did not significantly alter the predictive capacity of spindles during the initial cycles of sinusoidal movement (Dimitriou, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from Dimitriou, 2014.

claim: Peripheral (reflexive) input to γ neurons, including from cutaneous afferents, has been mainly demonstrated using electrical nerve stimulation in anaesthetized cats.
source: Peripheral ('reflexive') input to γ neurons, including from cutaneous afferents, has been mainly demonstrated using electrical nerve stimulation in anaesthetized cats (Appelberg et al., 1977; Johansson and Sojka, 1985; Johansson et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in cats.

claim: Pools of γ motor neurons should be considered as an integrative system able to combine descending commands and peripheral multisensory information.
source: These findings reinforce the idea that pools of γ motor neurons should be considered as an integrative system able to combine sensorimotor 'apples and oranges', that is, descending commands and peripheral multisensory information.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited findings about peripheral input to γ neurons.

claim: A functional degree of peripheral multisensory integration may be possible at the level of the spindle as a result of afferent control of γ neurons.
source: A functional degree of peripheral multisensory integration – such as for dexterous object manipulation – may be possible at the level of the spindle as a result of afferent control of γ neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional significance of peripheral control.

claim: This hypothesis is compatible with evidence of multimodal signals (tactile-proprioceptive) already in area 3a of the somatosensory cortex.
source: This hypothesis is compatible with evidence of 'multimodal' signals (tactile-proprioceptive) already in area 3a of the somatosensory cortex (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2015.

claim: Cutaneous stimulation has been shown to have a limited impact in two studies of spindle afferent activity in passive humans.
source: However, so far, cutaneous stimulation has been shown to have a limited impact in two studies of spindle afferent activity in passive humans (Aniss et al., 1990; Gandevia et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aniss et al., 1990 and Gandevia et al., 1994.

claim: Afferent control of spindle sensitivity may prove stronger or more easily unmasked in the active individual.
source: But afferent control of spindle sensitivity may prove stronger or more easily unmasked in the active individual (e.g. due to higher background tonus).
evidence: This is speculation about potential differences between passive and active conditions.

claim: The specific functional advantage of having afferent connections to γ neurons is currently unclear.
source: The specific functional advantage of having such afferent connections is currently unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in understanding.

claim: One previous study has demonstrated edge-orientation processing in tactile neurons as a function of their receptive fields.
source: One previous study has demonstrated edge-orientation processing in tactile neurons as a function of their receptive fields (Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014.

claim: In the case of edge-orientation processing, cutaneous afferent signals were bound to the characteristics of the adequate physical stimulus.
source: However, in this case, cutaneous afferent signals were bound to the characteristics (edge-orientation) of the 'adequate' physical stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the findings from Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014.

claim: Muscle spindle output can potentially be modulated according to the characteristics of a physical stimulus in another modality via efferent control.
source: In contrast, muscle spindle output can potentially be modulated according to the characteristics of a physical stimulus in another modality (e.g. cutaneous), via efferent control.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about spindle function.

claim: The possibility of substantial peripheral control of fusimotor neurons adds another layer of support to the proposition that spindles are best viewed as flexible signal-processing devices.
source: Although top-down control alone supports the notion that spindles are best viewed as flexible signal-processing devices rather than basic mechanoreceptors (Figure 1B and Figure 2), the possibility of substantial peripheral control of fusimotor neurons adds another layer of support to this proposition.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of peripheral control.

claim: Peripheral modulation of spindle sensitivity may be enabled by the structure of these encapsulated organs.
source: While fusimotor innervation can allow spindles to function as controllable signal-processors, peripheral modulation of spindle sensitivity may be also enabled by the structure of these encapsulated organs.
evidence: This is speculation about structural contributions to spindle function.

claim: It has long been known in microneurography circles that percutaneous mechanical pressure applied near the spindle capsule can have some effect on spindle afferent firing.
source: It has long been known in microneurography circles that percutaneous mechanical pressure applied near the spindle capsule, likely leading to its compression, can have some effect on spindle afferent firing.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge within the microneurography community.

claim: Mechanical pressure can represent an ecologically valid stimulus brought on by increased intramuscular pressure due to active contraction or when muscles are palpated.
source: Such mechanical pressure can otherwise represent an ecologically valid stimulus, brought on by increased intramuscular pressure due to active contraction or simply materialize when muscles are palpated.
evidence: This is an inference about the ecological relevance of mechanical pressure.

claim: Spindle afferent responses to active movement are substantially affected by light-to-moderate percutaneous pressure applied near the spindle capsule.
source: Representative preliminary data from our lab indicate that, regardless of underlying mechanism, spindle afferent responses to active movement are substantially affected by light-to-moderate percutaneous pressure applied near the spindle capsule (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 as preliminary data.

claim: Intramuscular fluid pressure can have immediate and significant effects on contractile muscle force.
source: It is tempting to speculate as to the potential regulatory function of such peripheral modulation, especially in the context of recent findings that intramuscular fluid pressure can have immediate and significant effects on contractile muscle force (Sleboda and Roberts, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sleboda and Roberts, 2020.

claim: The findings in Figure 3 serve as an indication that spindles are inclined to produce flexible representations rather than a consistent picture of actual limb kinematics.
source: Nevertheless, the preliminary findings in Figure 3 serve as yet another indication that spindles are inclined to produce flexible representations rather than a consistent picture of actual limb kinematics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the preliminary data in Figure 3.

claim: Muscle spindle organs are versatile signal-processing devices whose overarching role is to facilitate sensorimotor performance according to task characteristics.
source: I propose that muscle spindle organs are versatile signal-processing devices whose overarching role is to facilitate sensorimotor performance according to task characteristics, rather than faithfully encode posture and movement.
evidence: This is the author's main proposal, based on inference from the presented evidence.

claim: The complete spindle repertoire remains to be revealed.
source: The complete spindle repertoire remains to be revealed.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The fusimotor neurons controlling spindles can integrate multisensory peripheral input and top-down commands.
source: The fusimotor neurons controlling spindles can integrate multisensory peripheral input and top-down commands (which can also reflect sensory events, e.g. in vision; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on the evidence presented, including Figure 2D.

claim: It is reasonable to think of fusimotor activity as an intermediate coordinate transformation enabling different information to converge on spindles.
source: It is reasonable to think of fusimotor activity as an intermediate coordinate transformation enabling different information to converge on spindles, generating flexible coordinate representations at level of the PNS (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Dimensionality reduction via spindle processing may potentially simplify motor control without limiting performance.
source: Such dimensionality reduction may potentially simplify motor control without limiting performance.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional benefits of the proposed model.

claim: A more flexible and central role for spindles justifies the premium placed on their control by the nervous system.
source: A more flexible and central role for spindles justifies the premium placed on their control by the nervous system (i.e. ~30% of lower motor neurons are γ).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the proposed role to the anatomical investment in spindle control.

claim: A flexible role for spindles is compatible with models that claim the motor cortex essentially operates in proprioceptive coordinates.
source: Such a role is also compatible with the seemingly large number of parameters found to correlate closely with motor and premotor neural activity, and with models that claim the motor cortex essentially operates in 'proprioceptive' coordinates (Adams et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adams et al., 2013.

claim: Consistent information about actual limb position and movement kinematics is necessary.
source: Consistent information about actual limb position and movement kinematics is also necessary.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for sensorimotor function.

claim: How we sense our body depends on the interplay of multimodal signals.
source: It is widely believed that how we sense our body, including its position and movement, depends on the interplay of multimodal signals (e.g. Makin et al., 2008; Proske and Gandevia, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Makin et al., 2008 and Proske and Gandevia, 2012.

claim: Vision, joint and cutaneous signals contribute to proprioception and kinesthesia.
source: While spindles can encode limb position preferentially in certain contexts (e.g. Figure 2C), vision, joint and cutaneous signals also contribute to proprioception and kinesthesia (Collins and Prochazka, 1996; Collins et al., 2005; Sarlegna and Sainburg, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collins and Prochazka, 1996; Collins et al., 2005; Sarlegna and Sainburg, 2009.

claim: Both a flexible role for spindles and multimodal contributions to proprioception are supported by the general model proposed.
source: Both a flexible role for spindles and multimodal contributions to proprioception are supported by the general model proposed here (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the proposed model shown in Figure 4.

claim: Direct electrical stimulation of single joint and cutaneous afferents evokes appropriate sensations.
source: Interestingly, it is known that direct electrical stimulation of single joint and cutaneous afferents evokes appropriate sensations, but stimulation of single spindle afferents does not lead to any conscious sensations in the absence of movement (Macefield et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Macefield et al., 1990.

claim: Stimulation of single spindle afferents does not lead to any conscious sensations in the absence of movement.
source: Interestingly, it is known that direct electrical stimulation of single joint and cutaneous afferents evokes appropriate sensations, but stimulation of single spindle afferents does not lead to any conscious sensations in the absence of movement (Macefield et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Macefield et al., 1990.

claim: Tendon vibration of the unseen limb can lead to illusory perception of physically impossible limb configurations.
source: Tendon vibration (artificial spindle stimulus) of the unseen limb can lead to illusory perception of physically impossible limb configurations, and seeing the vibrated limb strongly attenuates illusory motion (Lackner and Taublieb, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lackner and Taublieb, 1984.

claim: Seeing the vibrated limb strongly attenuates illusory motion.
source: Tendon vibration (artificial spindle stimulus) of the unseen limb can lead to illusory perception of physically impossible limb configurations, and seeing the vibrated limb strongly attenuates illusory motion (Lackner and Taublieb, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lackner and Taublieb, 1984.

claim: If spindles are not routinely tasked with providing a faithful representation of posture and limb kinematics, spindle tuning can emphasize the flexible facilitation of concurrent or future action.
source: If spindles are not routinely tasked with providing a faithful representation of posture and limb kinematics (i.e., not tasked with encoding the consequences of action), spindle tuning can instead emphasize the flexible facilitation of concurrent or future action.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the proposed model.

claim: Elucidating the underlying mechanisms of spindle function in more detail will require much more work on multiple fronts.
source: While recording from human afferents and performing follow-up behavioral studies has helped shape our understanding of spindle function, elucidating the underlying mechanisms in more detail will require much more work on multiple fronts.
evidence: This is stated as a need for future research.

claim: Predictions stemming from human afferent data concerning fusimotor function can be tested more freely in animal models using a range of modern techniques.
source: For example, predictions stemming from human afferent data concerning fusimotor function can be tested more freely in animal models, using a range of modern techniques, as recently emphasized (Wilkinson, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilkinson, 2021.

claim: Achieving a comprehensive account of spindle contribution will likely advance our understanding of core sensorimotor principles.
source: Achieving a comprehensive account of spindle contribution will likely also advance our understanding of core sensorimotor principles.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications of understanding spindle function.

claim: Figure 2A shows averaged responses of a representative spindle afferent from the common digit extensor muscle during active sinusoidal movements of a single finger at 1Hz.
source: Averaged responses of a representative spindle afferent from the common digit extensor muscle, during active sinusoidal movements of a single finger at 1Hz (adapted from Figure 3 of Dimitriou, 2014).
evidence: This describes what is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Movement in the Figure 2A experiment was constrained to the metacarpophalangeal joint and occurred under a flexion resistive or assistive torque load, or no external load.
source: Movement was constrained to the metacarpophalangeal joint (MCP) and occurred under a flexion resistive or assistive torque load, or no external load.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for Figure 2A.

claim: Standard classification tests identified the afferent in Figure 2A as a typical spindle primary (type Ia).
source: Standard classification tests identified the afferent as a typical spindle primary (i.e. 'type Ia'; see Fig 2 in Dimitriou, 2014).
evidence: This describes the classification of the afferent shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Despite virtually identical finger flexion, spindle responses to stretch varied according to joint dynamics in the Figure 2A experiment.
source: Despite virtually identical finger flexion, spindle responses to stretch varied according to joint dynamics.
evidence: This is a key finding shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Figure 2B shows averaged spindle afferent population responses and equivalent muscle length changes during the classic visuomotor rotation task.
source: Averaged spindle afferent population responses and equivalent muscle length changes during the classic visuomotor rotation task (both 'B' and 'C' adapted from Figure 4A and 4E of Dimitriou, 2016).
evidence: This describes what is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Grey background bars in Figure 2B highlight phases in early adaptation that differ substantially from baseline.
source: Grey background bars highlight phases in early adaptation (orange) that differ substantially from baseline (black).
evidence: This describes a feature of Figure 2B.

claim: Correlating the signals shown in Figure 2B confirmed a significant relationship in the washout stage.
source: Correlating the signals shown in 'B' (down-sampled at 50ms) confirmed a significant relationship in the washout stage.
evidence: This describes the analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Figure 2D shows muscle velocity (null) and changes in spindle Ia responses before movement initiation in the classic instructed-delay reaching task with the hand.
source: Muscle velocity (null) and changes in spindle Ia responses before movement initiation in the classic instructed-delay reaching task with the hand.
evidence: This describes what is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ia firing rates from extensor muscles were lower when preparing movement to visual targets associated with stretch of the spindle-bearing muscle.
source: Ia firing rates from extensor muscles were lower when preparing movement to visual targets associated with stretch of the spindle-bearing muscle (purple).
evidence: This is a key finding shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Figure 2E shows averaged signals across participants from experiments using a robotic manipulandum that demonstrated congruent goal-directed tuning of stretch reflexes.
source: Averaged signals across participants; experiments using a robotic manipulandum showed a congruent goal-directed tuning of stretch reflexes, including at the short-latency epoch ('SLR') in cases where the homonymous muscle was not heavily loaded before perturbation.
evidence: This describes what is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Figure 3 shows responses of a spindle afferent from a wrist extensor muscle while the participant continuously moved their right semipronated hand about the wrist.
source: Responses of a spindle afferent from a wrist extensor muscle while the participant continuously moved their right semipronated hand about the wrist (flexion-extension; 0° denotes alignment with forearm).
evidence: This describes what is shown in Figure 3.

claim: In Figure 3, a hand-held probe was used to apply and measure mechanical pressure over a small area of skin on the forearm near the spindle capsule during some movement cycles only.
source: A hand-held probe was used by the experimenter for applying and measuring mechanical pressure over a small area of skin on the forearm (5 mm probe tip diameter), near the spindle capsule, during some movement cycles only (grey vertical bar denotes stimulus removal).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation shown in Figure 3.

claim: Despite very similar hand movement and activation patterns of the spindle-bearing muscle in Figure 3, spindle responses to hand flexion were markedly stronger during percutaneous pressure.
source: Despite very similar hand movement and activation patterns of the spindle-bearing muscle ('EMG'), spindle responses to hand flexion were markedly stronger during percutaneous pressure.
evidence: This is the key finding shown in Figure 3.

claim: Figure 4 shows that there can be independent descending control of γ dynamic and γ static spinal motor neurons in addition to descending commands to skeletal muscles and an efferent copy to forward models.
source: In addition to descending commands to skeletal muscles and an efferent copy to forward models (Figure 1A), there can be independent descending control of γ dynamic ('γd') and γ static ('γs') spinal motor neurons.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model shown in Figure 4.

claim: The vast majority of efferent projections to spindles are from γ motor neurons, but there is also some β supply.
source: The vast majority of efferent projections to spindles are from γ motor ('fusimotor') neurons, but there is also some β supply (indicated by the thinner dashed line).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and supported by earlier citations.

claim: Fusimotor control can affect spindle output in the absence of mechanical stimulation.
source: Fusimotor control can affect spindle output in the absence of mechanical stimulation (e.g. muscle stretch), but fusimotor activity can also shape spindle responses to direct mechanical stimulation arising from own action or the external environment.
evidence: This is a feature of the model shown in Figure 4.

claim: γ dynamic motor neurons project only to primary muscle spindles, allowing for differential control of primary and secondary muscle spindles.
source: '*': γd project only to primary muscle spindles, allowing for differential control of primary and secondary muscle spindles.
evidence: This is noted in Figure 4 and supported by earlier citations.

claim: Electrophysiological studies in mammals have demonstrated multisensory afferent convergence onto fusimotor neurons.
source: Electrophysiological studies in mammals have also demonstrated multisensory afferent convergence onto fusimotor neurons.
evidence: This is noted in Figure 4 and supported by earlier citations.

claim: The specific impact of afferent control of fusimotor neurons has not been determined yet in the active human and may vary across body segments.
source: '**': The specific impact of afferent control of fusimotor neurons has not been determined yet in the active human, and may well vary across body segments e.g., stronger in the hand and/or the foot.
evidence: This is noted in Figure 4 as a gap in knowledge.

claim: In the proposed model, joint and cutaneous receptors (and vision) provide consistent/reliable information about actual bodily state.
source: In this model, joint and cutaneous receptors (and vision) provide consistent/reliable information about actual bodily state, and potentially so do spindles, e.g., if they are predominantly affected by direct mechanical stimulation (as in the case of the passive, unengaged individual).
evidence: This is a feature of the model shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the proposed model, fusimotor activity represents an intermediate coordinate transformation that allows multimodal information to converge on spindles, creating flexible representations at the periphery.
source: But here, fusimotor activity represents an intermediate coordinate transformation that allows multimodal information to converge on spindles, creating flexible representations at the periphery.
evidence: This is the key feature of the model shown in Figure 4.

claim: Spindle tuning has been shown to facilitate load compensation in joint space, the selective extraction of information during motor adaptation, and the independent preparatory adjustment of reflexive muscle stiffness before goal-directed reaching.
source: So far, spindle tuning has been shown to facilitate load compensation in joint space, the selective extraction of information during motor adaptation, and the independent preparatory adjustment of reflexive muscle stiffness before goal-directed reaching (Figure 2).
evidence: This summarizes the findings shown in Figure 2.
